issue_context.title: FormFeature initialized with an IFormCollection instance throws NullReferenceException in Form property getter
issue_context.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

When the FormFeature type is constructed with an IFormCollection instance, the internal field _request is initialized to "default!" (null) in the ctor. When later accessing the Form property, a NullReferenceException is thrown from inside the private ResolveHasInvalidAntiforgeryValidationFeature() method, since it does not have a null guard for the _request field.

![image](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/assets/110810564/a1fb9af0-394c-4719-a24d-5914f28ce11e)


### Expected Behavior

The Form property should in this case return the IFormCollection used when constructing the instance of the FormFeature.

### Steps To Reproduce

_No response_

### Exceptions (if any)

NullReferenceException

### .NET Version

8

### Anything else?

_No response_
comments: @johatuni Thanks for opening this issue! Would you be interested in opening a PR to resolve this issue? Should be a matter of adding an null check to `ResolveHasInvalidAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.
Are there any workarounds for this issue?

> Are there any workarounds for this issue?

I changed my logic so that my controller unit tests could operate on an IFormCollection instance instead of a mock of the Request.Form property.

review_comments: We may want to try updating the nullability annotations on the `_request` field as well here.
Yes, that should probably be done too. It would be cleaner. But then there are a few more null checks missing in this type, I guess...

Yep -- it expands the scope of the PR a bit, but I figure this is the right time to do it while we have a motivating scenario.

If you don't have capacity to make the change, I'm happy to take a stab at it.
I can give it a go. Happy to contribute.

Personally, I think it would be clearer to check whether `contentType` is null (rather than testing `_request`) - the fact that a null `_request` yields a null `ContentType` seems like an implementation detail.
The idea here is that there might still be a `ContentType`, even if there's no request (i.e. as long as there's a form)?

The assumption is that if there's a form there will also always be a content type, and if there is both a request and a form, the request content type should take priority, if existing and valid. If there is no form and no request, the getter will return null.
